Trimps is the greatest spreadsheet micromanagement simulator to have ever been released for people who hyper fixate on greater integers becoming even greater. 

The only requirements needed are to have a basic understanding of both math and reading; everything else is just winging it, or gets automated in the future.

Trimps is a text‑based idle and incremental game where you manage a growing population of tiny creatures as they dig, fight and expand through an underground world. At its core, it’s a resource‑management sandbox: food, wood, metal, housing, population and time all feed into one another, creating a surprisingly deep progression loop.

Combat is one of the major tasks you can assign your Trimps. Equipment, research and upgrades steadily increase their battlefield strength. But the real strategic weight sits in how you allocate your population. You can only perform one direct action at a time, so the key is hiring and training Trimps to automate as many tasks as possible—gathering, building, fighting or simply staying idle to reproduce. Expanding your territory means constructing hubs and houses to raise your population cap, which in turn fuels every other system.

Game progress is suuuper slow. Active play is not about this game, most time you spend in this game you just wait when you collect enough resources for next upgrade which will NOT push you very far. 
In this game, in my opinion, there is not a geometric but an arithmetic progression. Even when you prestige and spend points to perks this will boost you like 10-20%, if you complete challenge reward will also give you like 10-20% boost. Yes it's an idler game, but usually most idler games let you feel that your decisions and time you spend let you progress much and much faster. I don't know how much time you need to spend to progress at least X2/X3 faster than when you can when just downloaded the game. 

It's good and not hard game, but too slow.
A deceptively deep and engaging game. I liken it to reading a novel. If you like idlers check it out. One of the very few games I've given money too.

Trimps is a text-based incremental and idle game that takes an extremely simple presentation and builds an unexpectedly elaborate progression system around it. Developed and published by Greensatellite, it places the player on a hostile planet with no memory and introduces the strange creatures known as Trimps as the foundation of both survival and expansion. Instead of relying on flashy graphics or constant manual interaction, the game focuses on resource management, optimization, automation, and the satisfaction of gradually transforming a primitive operation into an increasingly sophisticated machine.

This is a good Idler. I could talk about a lot, but it has the most impressive feature I ever seen on an idler game: It shows you the most efficient thing to buy amongst of the same type.

Instead of going mad with calculations nor ignoring it and just building whatever, the game tells you "Hey, buy this one, it its the best one for the thing you want to do". Fantastic.

neg.text: I don't regret my time spent on this game, but it also did not feel like it respected that time. The emerging mechanics are slow and grueling, and eventually you just kind of reach a point where you don't care to find out what comes next. There are scripts to speed it up, but even then, the journey is arduous. It's strange to give a negative review after so many hours, especially since this makes it rank in my top 5 idlers, but I don't know. I simply do not feel like it was worth it. I would struggle to genuinely recommend this to anyone except the most die hard of "slow, eternal idler" fans.

It's a little more interesting than watching windows processes run, but only a little.  If you really like repetitive gameplay for the sake of getting 100 achievements by restarting multiple times just to get that one achievement, then sure, go for it.  If you want to do something marginally constructive with your time instead of checking in on this back ground process, you're better doing anything, really.  At least it's not a clicker.
